title: Plantar Fasciitis: Why Your Heel Hurts Every Morning and What to Do About It
excerpt: Sharp heel pain on your first steps out of bed? Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common foot problems in India. Here is what causes it and how physiotherapy helps.
tags: plantar fasciitis, heel pain, foot exercises, arch pain, morning foot pain, physiotherapy
content:
If you hobble out of bed every morning with a sharp pain at the bottom of your heel, you are not alone. Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common foot conditions we treat at PhysioFix in JP Nagar, Bangalore. It affects everyone from long-distance runners to shopkeepers who spend all day on their feet.

The good news: most cases improve significantly with the right exercises and a few lifestyle changes. No surgery required.

What is plantar fasciitis?

The plantar fascia is a thick band of tissue that runs along the bottom of your foot, connecting your heel bone to your toes. Think of it like a bowstring that supports the arch of your foot. When this tissue gets irritated or develops small tears, it causes pain at the heel, especially with the first steps after resting.

In simple terms: the tissue gets overworked and inflamed. Not because of a single injury, but because of repeated stress that your body could not keep up with.

Who gets it?

Plantar fasciitis does not discriminate. But certain groups see it more often:

  • People who stand for long hours (teachers, retail workers, hairstylists)
  • Runners and joggers, especially those who increased their mileage quickly
  • People with flat feet or very high arches
  • Those who are overweight or have recently gained weight
  • Office workers who switched to walking or running after years of being sedentary

In India, we also see a lot of cases among people who walk barefoot on hard floors at home. The hard surface offers zero shock absorption, and your plantar fascia pays the price.

The classic symptoms

Most people with plantar fasciitis describe the same pattern:

  1. Sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning. This is the hallmark symptom. You step out of bed and feel like someone stabbed your heel with a nail. After a few minutes of walking, it eases up.
  2. Pain after sitting for a long time. Stand up from your desk after two hours and the heel pain comes back.
  3. Pain that gets worse over the day if you are on your feet a lot, or improves with rest and returns when you start walking again.
  4. Tenderness when you press the inner side of your heel.

If the pain has lasted more than a few weeks without improvement, it is time to see a physiotherapist rather than just hoping it goes away on its own.

What causes it?

The root cause is almost always repetitive strain. The plantar fascia can handle a certain amount of load, but when you exceed that consistently (new shoes, new workout routine, extra body weight, long hours standing), small micro-tears develop in the tissue.

Here is what makes it worse:

  • Tight calf muscles. When your calves are stiff, your ankle cannot bend properly. The plantar fascia compensates and takes extra load. This is the most common contributor.
  • Worn-out footwear. If your daily shoes have flat, compressed soles, they are not absorbing impact anymore.
  • Sudden changes in activity. Going from zero exercise to a 5K training plan in a week is a recipe for foot problems.
  • Prolonged standing on hard surfaces. Tile floors, concrete, marble. All of these are brutal on your feet over hours.

5 exercises that actually help

These are the exercises we prescribe at PhysioFix for plantar fasciitis patients. They target the root causes: tight calves, weak foot muscles, and a stiff plantar fascia.

1. Calf stretches (wall stretch)

Stand facing a wall. Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height. Step one foot back, keeping that leg straight and the heel pressed into the floor. Bend the front knee and lean forward until you feel a stretch in the back calf of your straight leg. Hold for 30 seconds. Repeat 3 times on each side. Do this first thing in the morning before you even take your first steps.

2. Plantar fascia massage

Sit in a chair and place a tennis ball (or a frozen water bottle for extra relief) under your arch. Roll it slowly from your heel to the ball of your foot. Apply moderate pressure. Do this for 2 to 3 minutes per foot. The frozen bottle works because the cold reduces inflammation while the rolling stretches the fascia.

3. Towel scrunches

Place a towel flat on the floor. Use only your toes to scrunch the towel toward you. Do 2 sets of 10 repetitions per foot. This strengthens the small intrinsic muscles of your foot that support the arch.

4. Heel raises

Stand with your feet hip-width apart. Slowly rise up onto your toes, hold for 3 seconds, and lower back down. Do 3 sets of 15. As this gets easier, do single-leg heel raises for a harder challenge. Strong calf muscles distribute load better and take pressure off the plantar fascia.

5. Plantar fascia stretch

Sit with one leg crossed over the other. Pull your toes back toward your shin with your hand until you feel a stretch along the bottom of your foot. Hold for 15 seconds. Repeat 10 times per foot. This directly stretches the inflamed tissue.

Home remedies that complement physiotherapy

  • Ice the heel. Roll your foot on a frozen water bottle for 10 to 15 minutes after activity. This reduces swelling and numbs the pain.
  • Wear supportive footwear indoors. Stop walking barefoot on hard floors. Get a pair of cushioned sandals or slippers with arch support for home use.
  • Try a night splint. This holds your foot in a flexed position overnight, preventing the plantar fascia from tightening up while you sleep. Many of our patients notice a big difference in their morning pain after a few weeks of using one.
  • Manage your weight. Every extra kilogram adds roughly 4 kilograms of force on your feet while walking. Even modest weight loss can significantly reduce heel pain.
  • Reduce high-impact activity temporarily. Swap running for swimming or cycling for a few weeks while your foot heals. You can come back to running once the pain subsides.

When should you see a physiotherapist?

If your heel pain has persisted for more than two weeks despite home care, book a session. A physiotherapist can assess your gait, identify biomechanical issues (like overpronation), and design a targeted recovery plan.

At PhysioFix, we also look at how your whole lower body moves, not just your foot. Tight hamstrings, weak glutes, and poor hip stability can all contribute to plantar fasciitis. Treating the foot in isolation often leads to the pain coming back.

In rare cases where conservative treatment does not work after three to six months, your doctor might discuss options like corticosteroid injections or, very rarely, surgery. But the vast majority of people recover fully with physiotherapy and the habits above.

The bottom line

Plantar fasciitis is painful, but it is not permanent. The combination of targeted stretching, strengthening exercises, proper footwear, and a gradual return to activity works for most people. The key is consistency. Doing these exercises once will not fix anything. But 15 minutes every day for six to eight weeks? That is where the real change happens.
